bull_bear.title: Bull — competitive strengths

bull_bear.body:
- Supply chain and raw material price risk — Volatility in steel, zinc and polymer prices, supply disruptions or logistics delays could affect input costs, production schedules, margins and timely project execution. Cost inflation in raw materials and logistics is separately flagged as able to compress project margins during execution. Mitigation rests on a diversified vendor base, strategic procurement, commodity monitoring, optimised inventory, alternative sourcing arrangements and revised costing models.
- Tender pricing pressure in EPC bidding — Intense competition in EPC bidding can lead to aggressive pricing, impacting margins and project viability. The Company's response is a disciplined and selective bidding approach focused on technically qualified opportunities with prudent pricing, choosing sustainable profitability over volume-led growth - which structurally caps how fast the order book can be grown.
- Execution delay risk — Delays arising from site conditions, supply disruptions or coordination gaps can extend project timelines and increase costs. Mitigated through detailed upfront planning, synchronized deployment, continuous monitoring, regional subcontractor networks and local stakeholder engagement.
- Multi-project execution risk across states — Simultaneous execution of projects across multiple states places pressure on equipment, technical resources and project management capability. Digital tracking systems, centralised escalation frameworks and structured resource deployment are used to monitor projects and reallocate resources - a risk that scales directly with the record order book.
- Technical and workplace safety risk — Transmission EPC projects involve high-voltage systems, difficult terrain, heavy equipment and complex erection activities, creating material technical and safety risks. In manufacturing, fabrication, galvanising, material handling and use of heavy machinery expose employees and contractors to occupational health and safety risks; a workplace injury or safety incident can disrupt operations, increase legal and regulatory liabilities and, per the BRSR, may in turn impact eligibility for certain contracts. Controls include standardised execution procedures, technical inspection protocols, ISO 45001-aligned safety management systems, fume extraction, PPE programmes, periodic safety audits and behavioural safety training across facilities and EPC sites.
- Regulatory and policy change risk — Changes in regulatory frameworks, bidding norms or project approvals can affect project timelines and pipeline visibility, and changes in environmental, labour, product quality or project-related regulations could increase compliance costs, delay approvals and affect operating continuity or reputation. Mitigated by a diversified project portfolio across clients and markets, participation in multiple bidding frameworks, relationships with government utilities and public sector organisations, and robust compliance systems with periodic audits.
- Climate transition, carbon regulation and energy cost risk — Manufacturing operations are energy-intensive and reliance on electricity and fossil fuels drives Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. Evolving regulations such as India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), together with energy price volatility, may influence compliance obligations, operating costs and competitiveness - CBAM is directly relevant given the export share of revenue. Physical climate risks including water stress, rising temperatures, extreme rainfall and flooding may impact operational continuity, infrastructure and supply chain reliability.
- Water availability and effluent management risk — Water is essential to several manufacturing processes including cooling, surface treatment and testing. Increasing water stress, changing rainfall patterns, tightening environmental regulations and rising stakeholder expectations could affect water availability, increase operational and treatment costs, disrupt production and elevate compliance and reputational risk.

outlook.body: FY26 was a capacity-building year for Skipper's engineering business. During the year the Company commissioned 75,000 MTPA of additional transmission tower manufacturing capacity, taking total installed capacity to 375,000 MTPA from 300,000 MTPA (which had been unchanged across FY24 and FY25), with the expanded capacity strengthening its ability to serve rising export demand and execute short-cycle domestic orders; capacity utilisation exceeded 85% during the year. outlook.body:
- Global T&D is entering a prolonged structural growth cycle driven by rising electricity demand, renewable integration, electrification of transport and industry, AI-led digital infrastructure, energy security initiatives and ageing grid assets
- Global electricity demand is projected to increase at an average annual rate of around 3.6% through 2030, significantly higher than the previous decade's average
- Annual investment in power infrastructure is projected to rise from approximately USD 631 billion in 2024 to nearly USD 1.1 trillion by 2050 (PwC Global Infrastructure Outlook), with cumulative investment of nearly USD 25 trillion; global grid investment reached nearly USD 450 billion in 2025
- Supply chain constraints, equipment shortages, longer lead times and permitting delays present execution challenges but simultaneously encourage capacity expansion, localisation of manufacturing and long-term procurement programmes by utilities - favouring established players with proven execution, manufacturing scale and global customer relationships
- North America: record utility capital expenditure programmes (~USD 1.3tn utility capex 2026-30) driven by AI-enabled data centres, electrification and replacement of ageing grid infrastructure; US data-centre electricity demand projected to reach ~75.8 GW by 2026 from ~53 GW in 2023
- Europe entering a significant grid investment cycle (EUR 1.2-1.4tn T&D capex 2026-35) for renewable integration, cross-border interconnection and modernisation of 40-50 year-old grids
- Middle East (particularly Saudi Arabia and the UAE) emerging as a growth market, with Saudi power-sector investment cited at ~USD 126bn/yr by 2035; strong opportunities for transmission equipment manufacturers and EPC companies
- Latin America (~USD 30bn/yr grid investment through 2035), Australia (10,000 km of new transmission lines planned against an 82% renewables-by-2030 target) and Africa provide additional long-term demand pools
- India: National Electricity Plan capex outlay of ₹9.2 trillion on high voltage transmission till FY 2032, driven by demand growth, RE integration and HVDC corridors
- Indian macro backdrop supportive: real GDP grew 7.7% in FY26 versus 7.1% in FY25, with PFCE and GFCF both above 7% growth; the World Bank has revised its FY27 growth estimate upward to approximately 6.6%
- Polymer demand driver: the polymer industry will witness sustained growth driven by rising demand for safe water infrastructure, housing expansion and increasing preference for certified, high-quality piping solutions, with a transition towards branded and organised players
- Polymer mix shift towards construction-led demand increased significantly during the year, improving demand stability and reducing exposure to seasonality-linked volatility
- Polymer margin levers: dynamic pricing, product mix management and operational efficiencies supported competitiveness amid volatility in PVC and CPVC input costs
- Risks flagged to the macro outlook: elevated energy prices, subsidy pressures on government spending, and uncertainty in global demand

risks.note: Delays arising from site conditions, supply disruptions or coordination gaps can extend project timelines and increase costs. Mitigated through detailed upfront planning, synchronized deployment, continuous monitoring, regional subcontractor networks and local stakeholder engagement.

Simultaneous execution of projects across multiple states places pressure on equipment, technical resources and project management capability. Digital tracking systems, centralised escalation frameworks and structured resource deployment are used to monitor projects and reallocate resources - a risk that scales directly with the record order book.

Transmission EPC projects involve high-voltage systems, difficult terrain, heavy equipment and complex erection activities, creating material technical and safety risks. In manufacturing, fabrication, galvanising, material handling and use of heavy machinery expose employees and contractors to occupational health and safety risks; a workplace injury or safety incident can disrupt operations, increase legal and regulatory liabilities and, per the BRSR, may in turn impact eligibility for certain contracts. Controls include standardised execution procedures, technical inspection protocols, ISO 45001-aligned safety management systems, fume extraction, PPE programmes, periodic safety audits and behavioural safety training across facilities and EPC sites.

Changes in regulatory frameworks, bidding norms or project approvals can affect project timelines and pipeline visibility, and changes in environmental, labour, product quality or project-related regulations could increase compliance costs, delay approvals and affect operating continuity or reputation. Mitigated by a diversified project portfolio across clients and markets, participation in multiple bidding frameworks, relationships with government utilities and public sector organisations, and robust compliance systems with periodic audits.

Manufacturing operations are energy-intensive and reliance on electricity and fossil fuels drives Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. Evolving regulations such as India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), together with energy price volatility, may influence compliance obligations, operating costs and competitiveness - CBAM is directly relevant given the export share of revenue. Physical climate risks including water stress, rising temperatures, extreme rainfall and flooding may impact operational continuity, infrastructure and supply chain reliability.

The Company's response is a disciplined and selective bidding approach focused on technically qualified opportunities with prudent pricing, choosing sustainable profitability over volume-led growth - which structurally caps how fast the order book can be grown.

Delays arising from site conditions, supply disruptions or coordination gaps can extend project timelines and increase costs. Mitigated through detailed upfront planning, synchronized deployment, continuous monitoring, regional subcontractor networks and local stakeholder engagement.

Simultaneous execution of projects across multiple states places pressure on equipment, technical resources and project management capability. Digital tracking systems, centralised escalation frameworks and structured resource deployment are used to monitor projects and reallocate resources - a risk that scales directly with the record order book.

Transmission EPC projects involve high-voltage systems, difficult terrain, heavy equipment and complex erection activities, creating material technical and safety risks. In manufacturing, fabrication, galvanising, material handling and use of heavy machinery expose employees and contractors to occupational health and safety risks; a workplace injury or safety incident can disrupt operations, increase legal and regulatory liabilities and, per the BRSR, may in turn impact eligibility for certain contracts. Controls include standardised execution procedures, technical inspection protocols, ISO 45001-aligned safety management systems, fume extraction, PPE programmes, periodic safety audits and behavioural safety training across facilities and EPC sites.

Changes in regulatory frameworks, bidding norms or project approvals can affect project timelines and pipeline visibility, and changes in environmental, labour, product quality or project-related regulations could increase compliance costs, delay approvals and affect operating continuity or reputation. Mitigated by a diversified project portfolio across clients and markets, participation in multiple bidding frameworks, relationships with government utilities and public sector organisations, and robust compliance systems with periodic audits.

risks.risk: Climate transition, carbon regulation and energy cost risk
risks.note: Manufacturing operations are energy-intensive and reliance on electricity and fossil fuels drives Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions. Evolving regulations such as India's Carbon Credit Trading Scheme (CCTS) and the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), together with energy price volatility, may influence compliance obligations, operating costs and competitiveness - CBAM is directly relevant given the export share of revenue. Physical climate risks including water stress, rising temperatures, extreme rainfall and flooding may impact operational continuity, infrastructure and supply chain reliability.

risks.risk: Water availability and effluent management risk
risks.note: Water is essential to several manufacturing processes including cooling, surface treatment and testing. Increasing water stress, changing rainfall patterns, tightening environmental regulations and rising stakeholder expectations could affect water availability, increase operational and treatment costs, disrupt production and elevate compliance and reputational risk.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Founded in 1981, Skipper Limited is India's largest manufacturer of transmission towers and ranked among the top five globally, operating an integrated power transmission & distribution engineering, EPC and polymer pipes platform.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: Skipper's engineering division manufactures transmission towers, monopoles, telecom towers, power distribution poles and railway electrification structures, supported by in-house steel rolling, CNC fabrication, galvanising, fastener manufacturing and full-scale tower testing. Its polymer division produces UPVC, CPVC, SWR, HDPE, agriculture and borewell pipes and fittings under the 'Skipper' brand for plumbing, sanitation and agricultural applications, sold through a pan-India retail network. A third infrastructure vertical provides EPC solutions spanning tower design, tower testing, manufacturing and onsite construction for power utilities, infrastructure developers and global EPC players.

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Global T&D is entering a prolonged structural growth cycle driven by rising electricity demand, renewable integration, electrification of transport and industry, AI-led digital infrastructure, energy security initiatives and ageing grid assets
- Global electricity demand is projected to increase at an average annual rate of around 3.6% through 2030, significantly higher than the previous decade's average
- Annual investment in power infrastructure is projected to rise from approximately USD 631 billion in 2024 to nearly USD 1.1 trillion by 2050 (PwC Global Infrastructure Outlook), with cumulative investment of nearly USD 25 trillion; global grid investment reached nearly USD 450 billion in 2025
- Supply chain constraints, equipment shortages, longer lead times and permitting delays present execution challenges but simultaneously encourage capacity expansion, localisation of manufacturing and long-term procurement programmes by utilities - favouring established players with proven execution, manufacturing scale and global customer relationships
- North America: record utility capital expenditure programmes (~USD 1.3tn utility capex 2026-30) driven by AI-enabled data centres, electrification and replacement of ageing grid infrastructure; US data-centre electricity demand projected to reach ~75.8 GW by 2026 from ~53 GW in 2023

- Middle East (particularly Saudi Arabia and the UAE) emerging as a growth market, with Saudi power-sector investment cited at ~USD 126bn/yr by 2035; strong opportunities for transmission equipment manufacturers and EPC companies
- Latin America (~USD 30bn/yr grid investment through 2035), Australia (10,000 km of new transmission lines planned against an 82% renewables-by-2030 target) and Africa provide additional long-term demand pools
- India: National Electricity Plan capex outlay of ₹9.2 trillion on high voltage transmission till FY 2032, driven by demand growth, RE integration and HVDC corridors
- Indian macro backdrop supportive: real GDP grew 7.7% in FY26 versus 7.1% in FY25, with PFCE and GFCF both above 7% growth; the World Bank has revised its FY27 growth estimate upward to approximately 6.6%

- Polymer mix shift towards construction-led demand increased significantly during the year, improving demand stability and reducing exposure to seasonality-linked volatility
- Polymer margin levers: dynamic pricing, product mix management and operational efficiencies supported competitiveness amid volatility in PVC and CPVC input costs

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: FY26 was a capacity-building year for Skipper's engineering business. During the year the Company commissioned 75,000 MTPA of additional transmission tower manufacturing capacity, taking total installed capacity to 375,000 MTPA from 300,000 MTPA (which had been unchanged across FY24 and FY25), with the expanded capacity strengthening its ability to serve rising export demand and execute short-cycle domestic orders; capacity utilisation exceeded 85% during the year. To support its long-term growth strategy the Company is undertaking another 75,000 MT engineering capacity expansion, described as progressing well, which is expected to take total installed capacity to 450,000 MTPA. Management frames capacity creation under a disciplined capital allocation framework of three principles - capacity expansion only against a clear utilisation roadmap, order acceptance only when minimum EBITDA threshold requirements are met, and prudent working capital management through disciplined control of receivables and inventory - and states that competition risk is addressed partly by pursuing strategic capacity expansion through optimisation of existing facilities as well as greenfield and brownfield initiatives. Beyond manufacturing capacity, the Company is expanding its infrastructure footprint across high voltage transmission line, power substation, railway electrification, telecom and water management projects. Capacity growth is underpinned by an all-time high closing order book of ₹85,019 million as of March 31, 2026 (90% domestic, 10% export), record annual order inflow of over ₹56,780 million, 25 high voltage transmission projects under execution for PGCIL including 800 KV Khavda HVDC and several 765 kV and 400 kV transmission line projects, approximately 5,000 circuit kilometres of EHV and HVDC transmission line currently under execution, and an all-time high bidding pipeline exceeding ₹33 billion. Long-term debt at the close of FY26 stood at ₹5,426 million against ₹3,071 million at the beginning of the year, an increase management attributes to the funding architecture of a capital-intensive business in a high-growth phase. The rupee quantum of capital expenditure is not stated: the Capital Commitments and Segment Capital Expenditure named-disclosure blocks in this bundle carry headings only, with no readable figures, units or attributable periods.

- Integrated manufacturing model with a high degree of backward integration - about 90% of raw materials sourced in house - covering design and engineering, steel rolling, CNC fabrication, galvanising, fasteners, testing and EPC execution, resulting in competitive cost structures and enhanced margins
- India's largest transmission tower manufacturer with a significant share in high-voltage segments (400 kV and above); described as India's leading and world's only integrated T&D company
- Seven in-house automated galvanising plants and four Power Grid approved plants
- Testing moat: NABL-accredited facility with full-scale tower and pole load testing at Bagnan; commissioning of Test Bed 2 made Skipper the world's only company with dual test bed facilities, plus a first-of-its-kind integrated tower testing set-up for lattice towers and monopoles
- Engineering firsts: first Indian company to design and supply transmission monopoles and guyed towers to North America; conducted India's first ever testing of CICA (Composite Insulated Cross Arms); prototyped and tested the world's heaviest transmission tower weighing 293 MT
- Export reach across 65+ countries with long-standing relationships with more than 300 global EPC clients and utilities
- Polymer distribution depth: more than 110 distributors, 4,050 dealers, over 4,860 multi-brand outlets and over 31,000 retail touchpoints across India, with a strong retail footprint in Eastern and Northeastern India
- Influencer ecosystem in polymer: engagement with more than 1.25 lakh plumbers, with over 28,000 unique plumbers onboarded to its banking ecosystem
- Brand investment: 'India's Safest Pipes' campaign and onboarding of cricketer M.S. Dhoni as brand ambassador
- Strategic partnership with Lubrizol, the global pioneer of CPVC technology, to manufacture next generation CPVC piping systems using TEMPRITE technology
- Advanced manufacturing technology - a significant portion of production executed on automated CNC machinery and modern fabrication lines - strengthened in FY26 by implementation of SAP S/4HANA RISE and increased digital integration
- Capacity built ahead of opportunity: 75,000 MTPA commissioned in FY26 taking engineering capacity to 3,75,000 MTPA with capacity utilisation exceeding 85%
- Diversified presence across utilities, infrastructure, telecom, renewable energy and retail markets, which the Company states enhances business resilience

risks.title: Risks & watch-items
risks.body:
- **Exports / Middle East**: order inflow & execution hit by geopolitics; timing of recovery unclear — primary reason for soft FY27 guide.
- **Trade receivables doubling** to INR 1,485 cr — monitor realization despite mgmt reassurance.
- **ROW / forest clearances**: on-ground execution slippage vs scheduled timelines.
- **Critical-equipment shortage** (transformers, HVDC) — global, throttles system commissioning & bidding pace; not within Skipper's control.
- **Bidding timing risk**: FY27 awarding ramp is the key catalyst; any further CEA/PFC-REC delay pushes the re-acceleration.
- Polymer margins stuck in low single digits; sub-scale vs national players.
- Sea-freight inflation slowing export customers' decision-making.

non_obvious.title: Non-obvious takeaways
non_obvious.body:
- 30% PAT growth is "locked" from existing order book quality, decoupled from new-order timing — a high-conviction earnings floor regardless of bidding lull.
- The FY26 bidding slowdown was deliberate (CEA "purposely held back" due to backlog + equipment shortage), not demand weakness — implies pent-up FY27-28 surge, not structural decline.
- Substation entry quietly doubles TAM (lines 50% → +substations 50%); margins claimed similar, not dilutive as analyst assumed.
- Dual test-bed + world-record tower testing is a genuine, hard-to-replicate qualification moat for large international (developed-market) orders.
- Receivable spike is largely a March-end technical slip (INR 260 cr) + domestic-mix shift, not deterioration — but worth verifying next quarter.
- Non-T&D/infra now negligible (14%, mostly BSNL O&M) — company is essentially a pure-play T&D structures manufacturer now.

strategy.title: Strategies (RHP)
strategy.body:
- Transition the polymer business from a pipes manufacturer to a full-spectrum water-management / integrated plumbing systems brand, extending the safety and quality promise across pipes, fittings, tanks and bath systems
- Drive premiumisation through CPVC and value-added products, and manage product mix towards higher-value offerings to support margin stability
- Expand distribution across core, growth and seed markets using a structured market-segmentation framework, with deliberate depth in Tier II, Tier III, rural and semi-urban towns
- Integrate influencers into the demand model through plumber …

order book & pipeline:
- Closing order book INR 8,501.9 cr; mix 90% domestic / 10% export.
- Bidding pipeline >INR 33,000 cr (~60-65% domestic, 35-40% export); historical conversion 20-25%.
- Large multimillion-dollar order won from a leading North American utility (developed-market breakthrough).

segment / subsidiary:
- **Engineering** (~78% of FY26 rev): core T&D, leading growth, ~100% EHV (400/765/800 kV), almost all sales now T&D (legacy low-margin non-T&D phased down → margin uplift).
- **Polymer** INR 507 cr, +~40% volume but value growth lower (commodity deflation); margins still low single-digit; double-digit aspiration as revenue approaches INR 700-1,000 cr; still Eastern-region-concentrated, slowly expanding North/West.
- **Infra / non-T&D**: now only ~14% of order book; order book declined INR 2,000 cr → ~INR 1,000 cr over 6-7 quarters; largely BSNL O&M; de-emphasized.
growth verticals / optionality:

- Operating leverage at >85% utilization is the core margin lever; incremental volume = higher margin.
- Better product mix (more 765 kV, HVDC, monopoles, T&D-only) lifting margins; aspirational 12% EBITDA.
- 100% indigenous raw material — no import/supply disruption.

- Freight: only ~10% export book + FOB/CIF mix + force-majeure renegotiation → ocean-freight spike not a margin risk.
